items.description: Per analysis 033 — under phases + priority, the engine can count passes per agent per phase per meeting. Wire this into the synthetic-consensus guard (already exists) and add new detectors: never-passes (sprawl shape), always-passes-after-first-utterance (withdrawal shape). The substrate gains an outside-the-agent measurement primitive for §VIII failure modes that currently can only be inferred post-hoc from the transcript.

items.title: Two-Headed Giant: team windows for constitutional pairs
items.description: Per the live r35-tdd-serial-phased run: strict-serial priority gate inside a rotation accidentally serializes constitutional pairs that are complementary, not adversarial (Tweedledee:frontend :: Tweedledum:backend; Alice:user-journey :: Hatter:failure-mode). Wall-clock cost ~N× cast size for the same deliberation depth. Fix: extend PhaseSpec with team_groupings: list[list[str]], default one-agent-per-team (current behavior). A team window opens concurrently for all members via asyncio.gather; per-agent WindowOutcome preserves §VIII observability primitives. Phase advances when all teams pass in succession. Maps onto MtG's Two-Headed Giant format. Substantive but local: orchestrator changes, no new event surface needed.

items.title: Agent-to-user questions: ask_user / interactive escalation
items.description: Per the live r35-tdd-serial-phased run: Alice's grounding instinct produced a coherent reframe of the daily-review feature (Pomodoro session review → reflective journaling), accumulated across stories 015-017. The reframe is actually a product insight worth surfacing — but the substrate has no channel for 'this might be a different product than you specified, does that resonate?' before the team commits to the new direction. Build agent → user question affordance: agent emits a question addressed to the user (likely a new speech_act QUESTION_TO_USER or a tool ask_user(prompt)->answer), runtime pauses, TUI surfaces with text-input prompt, answer reflows into the agent's deliberation context. Builds on existing Runner._pending_escalations machinery and human-in-the-loop escalation already done in P2 (39a91906). For phased meetings, the window resolves as act/pass/ask; ask pauses without consuming the window, agent re-deliberates with the answer. Solves a class of problems: Alice's product reframes, Tweedles' contract ambiguities, Caterpillar's actionable-vs-fast-follow judgment calls.

items.title: Decouple structural cap from meeting_budget in phased runs
items.description: Per analysis 035 F2: meeting_budget gate fires inside run_phased_meeting's inner loop and truncates phases mid-flight (10 of 18 phases in r36 aborted this way; M6 defend never opened). Phases should run to structural completion (rotation cap / succession / exit_condition); meeting_budget moves to _run_one_meeting as a between-meetings check. Lets the TDD red→green→fix-on-review loop actually complete on review findings. Operator's stated preference: quality > cost, so deferring is fine; flagged P2.

items.title: Phased orchestrator: respect runner.budget_dollars global cap
items.description: Per analysis 035 F7: runner.budget_dollars is enforced via budget_exceeded events on runner.events() in legacy _convene_one, but run_phased_meeting doesn't drain runner.events() — it owns deliberation via compose_context + deliberate. r36 declared 5 cap and hit 8.85 (77% over); r35 hit 7.88 (58% over). Fix: ~10 LOC, check runner.total_cost >= runner.budget_dollars at top of phased inner loop, set outcome=GLOBAL_BUDGET, break+propagate. Operators who declare 5 should be able to trust 5 is the ceiling.

items.title: Housekeeping: scrub trademarked 'Two-Headed Giant' refs to 'team windows'
items.description: Per a public-PR readiness pass: 'Two-Headed Giant' is a Wizards of the Coast trademark (MtG format name); the project's references should use a generic 'team windows' or 'Teams' framing. Sweep needed across: filename analyses/035-tdd-phased-teams-2hg-first-run.md (rename to drop -2hg); analyses 033 + 034 prose where I introduced the term; gameplan phase id p9.5-two-headed-giant (rename to p9.5-team-windows); roadmap item dbf88619 title; closet/workflows/tdd-serial-phased.yaml comments; src/wonderland/meeting.py + turns.py code comments (a handful of MtG / 2HG mentions). Functional behavior unchanged; this is rename-only.

items.title: Skeleton auto-install runner: execute manifest.post_apply commands
items.description: Per T73's manifest layer. Add an apply-then-install path that runs the skeleton's post_apply commands as subprocesses with progress reporting in the SkeletonPickerScreen. Considerations: long-running installs (pip 1-5min, npm 5-15min) need a non-blocking UI; failures need clear surfacing; venv creation may need to be a separate step. Defer until a operator wants unattended-capable runs against fresh project roots without touching a shell. The manifest from T73 makes this tractable when we want it.

items.title: Run-follow hook: active-run pointer + daedalus run follow CLI
items.description: Lets Claude/Daedalus observe live runs without operator interruption to paste paths. Two pieces: (1) NewRunScreen / LiveRunHandle writes ~/.wonderland/current_run.txt on launch with the snapshot path, clears it on RunEnded. (2) daedalus run follow CLI tails phase-events.jsonl + tool-calls.jsonl + the latest telemetry/run-*.json, prints meaningful summaries (PhaseStarted -> 'M4.clarify started, 4 cast'; AgentActed -> 'tweedledum acted in window 3'; cost-tick when total_cost crosses /bin/bash.50 boundaries; write_file -> 'src/api.py +200 LOC'). Reads from current_run.txt if no explicit path. Future: server-side hook for richer integrations (slack notifications on milestones, webhook on completion); for now, polling-via-Bash from the agent side covers the use case.

items.title: Claude Code skill: wonderland run follow
items.description: Wraps the daedalus run follow CLI (roadmap 6287eff9) as a Claude Code skill so any Claude session can invoke /wonderland-follow (or similar) to observe an active run without bash-polling boilerplate. Skill discovers current_run.txt, tails the JSONL files, returns formatted progress summaries to the agent. Supports per-call snapshot path override for inspecting historical runs. Lives in .claude/skills/ or .claude/commands/ depending on how the project surfaces user-invocable skills. Composable with the existing daedalus and memory subagents.

items.title: Parallelize M4 (test_scenarios) per_item iterations
items.description: Per the analysis-037 wall-clock investigation: M4 iterations are structurally independent — each iter sees one feature's spec + contracts touching it, and produces test_scenarios + test files written to feature-slug-named paths (tests/test_<slug>_*.py). No shared state, no cross-iter file conflicts. Easy parallelization: in run_workflow, when meeting.per_item is set AND meeting opts in (new field: parallel_iterations: bool = false), replace the serial for-loop over items with asyncio.gather of _run_one_meeting calls. Each iteration gets its own thread_id (already established as {meeting.id}-{slug}). For 5-feature pomodoro, M4 wall-clock drops ~5x (from ~30 min serial to ~6 min parallel). Supersedes the generic 0b785ab0; M5 parallelization is filed separately (more complex).

items.title: Parallelize M5 (implementation) per_item iterations
items.description: Per the analysis-037 wall-clock investigation. M5 parallelization is non-trivial because iterations share infrastructure: src/store.py, src/api.py route registration, src/models.py schema. Two iterations writing to the same file race; run_tests called concurrently can hit pytest collection races, port collisions for FastAPI servers, fixture state clobbering. Path forward (in order): (1) detect file-conflict via a shared-files declaration on contracts; serialize iters that touch the same files. (2) Sandbox run_tests per-iteration with per-iter pytest fixtures + port pools. (3) Allow per-meeting parallelism opt-in via parallel_iterations field with a max_concurrent cap. Or simpler: ship M5 sequentially even when M4 parallelizes (M4 is the bigger wall-clock chunk anyway), and leave M5 as future work. Lower priority than M4 because the wins are smaller and the implementation is harder. Supersedes the M5 portion of generic 0b785ab0.

items.title: Hatter test-file scaffolding in skeletons (output-share optimization)
items.description: Per analysis 038 token-share investigation: Hatter's output share is 33% of agent cost vs ~20% for Tweedles, because Hatter writes new test files (write_file dumps full file content as output tokens at $5/MTok). Diff tool can't help when the file doesn't exist yet. Mitigation: extend the skeleton bundle system (T70-T73) so each skeleton ships per-feature test stub scaffolding — placeholder test files Hatter can str_replace into instead of creating from scratch. Concretely: a skeleton manifest field like 'test_stub_template' that the M3-output 'feature contract' triggers — when contract-note-NNN-<slug>.md lands, generate a tests/test_<slug>_<phase>.py stub from the template (red-by-default test markers, fixture imports already wired). Hatter then str_replaces real assertions in. Should pull Hatter output share toward 20% (Tweedle-equivalent) and side-effect: keeps Hatter on-task by giving structural cues for what each feature's tests should look like. Bundle-level work — applies to fullstack, python-fastapi, python-cli, python-tui equally.

items.title: git_diff defaults to --stat; full diff opt-in via separate tool
items.description: Per analysis 038 token-share investigation: Tweedles spend 19.3% (tweedledee) and 19.2% (tweedledum) of bytes-through-context on git_diff. Diffs change turn-to-turn so they're mostly uncached, hitting full $1/MTok input rate. Mitigation: change the default git_diff Tools.git_diff() shape to return --stat output (file paths + LOC delta counts) instead of full patch. Tweedles can still inspect specifics via a new git_diff_full tool when they need the patch content. Two-call pattern (stat first, full-on-demand) saves tokens on the common case where the agent just needs to know which files changed how much. Same shape as how senior engineers actually skim diffs — read --stat first, only zoom in when something looks interesting. Estimated savings: if 70% of git_diff calls were satisfied by --stat alone, Tweedle git_diff cost share drops from 19% to ~6% (input bytes drop ~10x for stat vs full diff).

items.title: Investigate 1-hour cache writes for long M5 iterations (uncached input share)
items.description: Per analysis 038 token-share investigation: ~30% of Tweedles+Hatter cost is uncached input — first-time file reads OR content that fell out of the 5-minute prompt cache window. Suspected cause: long M5 iterations with Caterpillar reviews in the loop can pause >5min between same-file reads, forcing re-pay on first read. Investigation: instrument the LLMClient to log time-since-last-cache-hit per file path. If clustering shows frequent gaps in [5min, 60min] range, switch cache_control 'ttl' from default 5m to 1h (priced at $2/MTok cache write instead of $1.25/MTok, but valid 12x longer). Net savings if cache hits at 1h are >2x what they'd have been at 5m. Could be configurable per-meeting or per-agent (Tweedles benefit most because they iterate slowly across long phases). Anthropic's 1h cache only valid since claude-3-5-sonnet-v2 onwards; verify Haiku 4.5 supports it before designing.

items.title: Notify operator when auto-sentinel timer is about to fire / has fired
items.description: Per analysis 038 F3: r40 was unattended; team STUCK on main thread + Dodo escalated; auto-sentinel (T69 follow-up) presumably fired since outcome=complete, but the operator received no notification (no toast, no system-level alert) signalling that human input was being requested. Operator's mental model — 'I'll get a notification if the team needs me' — didn't hold. Two failure modes worth investigating: (1) auto-sentinel fired silently and resolved the deadlock without surfacing the question in operator-visible UI; (2) no sentinel fired; the run terminated via budget-exceeded path independently of the user-question affordance. Either way: for unattended runs to be reliable, the operator needs *some* signal when a question is pending past the auto-sentinel timer. Implementation: (a) Textual notification + native OS notification via notify-send / equivalent when AskUserModal pushes; (b) audible chime option (configurable via Settings); (c) terminal bell as zero-dependency fallback; (d) in the run's final report, surface 'auto-sentinel fired N times during run' so operator can audit unattended decisions post-hoc. T69 followup; touches LiveRunScreen + ask_user_modal.py.

items.title: Tighten primer for operator questions; add M2.5 mandatory checkpoint
items.description:
Per r39, r40, r41-obol: third confirmed instance of agents NOT using the operator-question affordance even when warranted. Cat's r41-obol ADR literally names a question ('does the user expect this to run on a single machine, or be networked/multi-access?') and then declines to ask, leaving it as a tradeoff. Zero QUESTION utterances in the bus across all three runs. Affordance works in code (T69); agents just aren't using it.

Root cause: constitutional hint at primer.py:130-143 over-corrects. Reads as 'use sparingly, prefer M3 contract negotiation, prefer M2.5 composition, the operator is not a fallback...' which agents interpret as 'asking the operator is borderline forbidden.' They always defer to the team, even on questions only the operator can answer (external service auth, single-vs-multi-user assumption, scope-defining UX preferences).

Two-part fix:

(1) Reframe primer.py:130-143 from 'use sparingly' to 'ask whenever a decision affects deliverable shape and the team lacks information the operator has.' Concrete trigger examples: external service authentication patterns (sandbox vs live tokens), single-vs-multi-user / single-machine-vs-networked assumptions, scope-defining UX preferences (anomaly thresholds, what 'recent' means, density vs hierarchy in TUI). Counter-examples: don't ask about implementation details that contracts can express; don't ask when team-internal deliberation can resolve.

(2) Add an explicit M2.5 checkpoint to Caterpillar's directive in tdd-serial-phased.yaml (and other phased workflows): 'If you finish this phase without naming at least one question for the operator, justify why none exist.' Forces the affordance into the deliberative loop. M2.5 is the right phase because composition is when ambiguities surface as 'this claim about scope doesn't hold yet' — exactly the shape that should escalate.

Validation: a run on a directive with genuinely-ambiguous external surface (Plaid integration, payment flow, content moderation rules) should produce at least one QUESTION-to-operator utterance. r42-obol-redux or a synthetic re-run of the obol directive after this ships is the natural test.

items.title: Skeleton hello-worlds shouldn't ship domain-named example code (skeleton parasitism)
items.description:
Per analysis 039 (r41-obol failure): when a skeleton ships executable example code with named domain artifacts (e.g. python-tui's CounterScreen + counter-label widget + 'Count: N' UI text + tests asserting on the counter), the team can't tell where 'skeleton hello-world' ends and 'operator's actual project' begins. The example code becomes the project. r41-obol shipped 0 LOC of personal-finance code; instead Tweedles + Caterpillar spent M5/M6 fixing the python-tui skeleton's broken counter-app tests.

Analysis 037 reframed skeleton-as-substrate as load-bearing for production-code shape (good). r41 reveals the failure mode at the OTHER end of the curve: too much skeleton scaffolding, with domain semantics, parasitizes the team's attention.

Two-part fix:

(1) Audit existing skeletons (python-cli, python-fastapi, python-tui, react-vite, fullstack-fastapi-react) — replace domain-named example code with unmistakably-placeholder shapes. Examples:
  - python-tui: drop CounterScreen entirely; ship a one-screen 'Hello' stub with a class named _SkeletonPlaceholderScreen and a comment explicitly saying 'replace this in your first feature'
  - python-cli: drop any worked Click command; ship a single empty  group with one  subcommand
  - python-fastapi: keep the /health endpoint (system-level, not domain) but drop any /hello or /counter/items style example
  - fullstack: same logic both halves

(2) README guidance: every skeleton README should have a 'What's intentionally left to your project' section listing what isn't there yet (e.g. 'No screen — pick yours; the placeholder demonstrates the wiring but should be deleted in your first feature'). Set the expectation that the placeholder gets DELETED, not extended.

Validation: a re-run of the obol directive on python-tui should produce a personal-finance app, not a counter app.

items.title: M2.5 needs structural exit condition: must produce >=1 feature or escalate
items.description:
Per analysis 039 (r41-obol): M2.5 (composition) is phase-free per the tdd-serial-phased workflow, which means in engagement-policy mode the meeting can close even if White Rabbit emits zero features. r41-obol's M2.5 thread had 5 utterances total: alice|story (seed), white_rabbit|ticket (seed), dodo|directive, dodo|nudge, dodo|acknowledgment. Rabbit was silent. The team proceeded through M3-M6 working off ticket seeds via 'from: any' fallback, which produced contracts but no features-shaped deliverable.

The workflow's M2.5 directive is extremely clear about stakes: 'Without features, M3 has nothing to negotiate' (line 187). But the workflow lacks a structural enforcement mechanism. The directive can be ignored without consequence in the current run.

Two implementation options:

(a) Phased-mode M2.5 with exit_condition_artifact: feature. The phased orchestrator already supports exit conditions (T57 / PhaseSpec.exit_condition_artifact). Setting this on M2.5's single phase forces the meeting to keep convening windows until at least one feature lands or rotation cap is exhausted. Existing infrastructure; minimal code change.

(b) Workflow-level post-meeting validator: after M2.5's MeetingEndedEvent, count feature utterances on the composition thread. If zero, abort the run with a clear escalation (operator sees: 'M2.5 produced no features. The team needs guidance on what to ship — review tickets and re-run with a tighter directive, or escalate to operator'). Fails loud and gives the operator a useful next step instead of letting the run silently produce wrong-shaped output.

Recommendation: ship (a) first because it reuses existing phased-orchestrator machinery. (b) is the more general 'post-meeting invariant' surface and worth filing separately if it's needed for other meetings (e.g. M2 must produce >=1 ticket; M3 must produce >=1 contract per feature).

Validation: a re-run of the obol directive should either (i) produce features in M2.5, or (ii) cleanly escalate with a 'no features produced' outcome rather than letting the run drift into phantom-seed downstream work.

items.title: Background-run daemon: launch detached, close TUI without killing, re-attach later
items.description:
Today, a TUI run lives inside the TUI process. Close the TUI = kill the run. The operator can't switch terminals, can't survive an SSH disconnect, can't 'fire and check tomorrow.'

Goal: runs become first-class background processes the TUI attaches to, not children of the TUI.

Design surface:

(1) wonderland-runner daemon — separate process owning Runner + workflow loop. Launches via  or a TUI 'Launch detached' button. PID + run metadata in <project>/.wonderland/runner.pid. Status updates land in the existing phase-events.jsonl + telemetry/run-*.json (already on-disk substrate; LiveRunScreen already replays from these via the observer pattern).

(2) TUI re-attach — on launch, scan known projects' .wonderland/ for active PID files. If process is alive, surface 'Run in flight on <project>' in the project library; press enter to attach (LiveRunScreen wraps an existing-snapshot observer instead of constructing a fresh Runner). If PID is stale (process gone, no terminal RunEnded event in phase-events), show 'Aborted run; click to view final state.'

(3) Kill button — TUI sends SIGTERM (or writes a sentinel file the daemon polls) to request graceful shutdown. Runner.abort() already exists; the daemon hooks into it. Hard kill (SIGKILL) as a follow-up if graceful doesn't land within N seconds.

(4) Multi-attach — multiple TUI instances can attach to the same run via the read-only observer pattern. Useful for pair-program-style 'sit with the team' sessions. The bus → file translation is already one-way; concurrent readers are safe.

Pitfalls to design through:

- Operator-question affordance: in-process bus today does a Future round-trip. Daemon design needs filesystem-mediated questions: question utterance → operator-questions/pending-NNN.md, TUI watches the dir + responds → operator-questions/answered-NNN.md → daemon picks up the answer. inotify or 200ms polling either works.
- API key access: daemon spawns from TUI, inherits env. If launched standalone (e.g. systemd later), needs config-path resolution.
- Observer back-pressure: live phase-events.jsonl tailing has to handle restarts / file rotation.
- Run cleanup: if daemon dies between runs, stale PID file remains. TUI's process-alive check is the disambiguator.

Lays foundation for: scheduled runs ('start at 3am'), multi-run pipelines (P12 lifecycle's batch-implement workflow chains naturally), webhooks (run completion → external notification), Claude Code integration (skill that launches detached runs).

Sequencing: probably 3-4 tasks within a P13 phase — daemon scaffold, re-attach UX, question-affordance over filesystem, kill semantics. Worth opening when P12 lifecycle work is in flight, since the lifecycle states feed the 'what runs are queued / in-flight / completed' surface the dashboard needs anyway.

items.title: Analysis 040: include workflow rethink (M1-M8 reorder, Hatter→implement) as a section
items.description:
Per the P12 thread: while drafting tdd-design + tdd-implement workflow YAMLs, we identified two structural problems with the previous tdd-serial-phased shape that warrant a section in analysis 040 once the obol redux + post-fix runs land:

1. **Order was backwards: tickets before features.** Original M2 produced tickets, M2.5 composed features from them — post-hoc grouping. r43-obol's monolithic-feature collapse was a direct consequence: Rabbit's grouping decisions in M2.5 are a labeling exercise on top of already-decomposed work, prone to lumping. New shape: stories → features → tickets, matching how product → engineering decomposes naturally. Features-first means Rabbit composes from human-shaped stories (small N, natural cleavage); tickets are derived per feature (small N each, granularity stable).

2. **Architecture was too early: M1 had Cat ADRs alongside Alice stories.** Cat architecting from stories alone produced abstract ADRs that didn't ground in concrete features (r41-obol's ADR-001). Cat architecting from features + tickets produces grounded commitments (r42-obol's ADR-002 'three backend domains' matched the personas exactly). Same logic for Queen security pass — concrete material to threat-model against. Moved both to M4 in the new design phase.

3. **Hatter belongs in implementation, not design.** Tea Party (formerly M4) writes actual executable failing tests, not just scenario prose. That's the red phase of TDD's red-green-refactor — it lives in implementation, paired with Tweedles' green. New shape: M6 Tea Party (per ticket: Hatter writes failing test + Tweedle commits implementation contract) is part of tdd-implement, not tdd-design. Designed features ship without test scenarios; the operator's design dossier is leaner but the implementation phase preserves TDD's pairing dynamic.

Section title for 040: 'Workflow rethink: from tdd-serial-phased to tdd-design + tdd-implement'

Three sub-points:
- Why the order was wrong (data: r41 ADR-001 vs r42 ADR-002 grounding quality; r43 monolithic-feature collapse)
- The atom split (design = M1-M5, implement = M6-M8) and the iteration economics (cheap design loops, expensive implementation gated by operator)
- Hatter relocation (TDD red-green needs Hatter+Tweedle pairing, not separate phases)

Plus the substrate fixes that made the split possible:
- T85 lifecycle data layer (features can persist in 'designed' state across runs)
- T86 input filter (tdd-implement only iterates over queued features)  
- T87 output transitions (workflow-level state machine wiring)
- T88 ticket-level per_item granularity (Rabbit's feature decisions don't override orchestrator calibration)
- Cross-run continuity (seed-fallback in 0.3.0 makes the design→implement handoff structural rather than agent-discretion-dependent)

Validation: re-run obol with tdd-design followed by tdd-implement; compare per-feature LOC density, deliverable shape, cost. r-obol-design-then-implement is the natural test case.

items.title: Registry validation for artifact slug references
items.description:
Per the obol slug-mismatch issue (analysis 040 thread): currently artifact payload fields like FeaturePayload.tickets, TicketPayload.sources, ContractNotePayload references are LOOSE STRING SLUGS with no validation. Rabbit can list 'balance-dashboard-v1' in feature.tickets and there's no check that any ticket with that slug exists in the registry.

Fix: validate slug references at write time. When TicketRegistry.write() is called, verify all sources slugs reference existing artifacts (in features registry, stories registry, etc. as appropriate per kind). When FeatureRegistry.write() is called, validate sources slugs (against stories) and tickets slugs (against tickets registry, OR allow empty-with-flag if M3 hasn't run yet). Rejection on mismatch.

Implementation considerations:
- Pydantic doesn't naturally support context-dependent validation (registry lookup needs project_root). Options: (a) move validation out of payload into the Registry.write() call, (b) use Pydantic v2 ContextManager pattern, (c) add a separate validate_against_registry() pass.
- Bidirectional: stories have no upstream; tickets validate against features+stories; features validate against stories (and against tickets when emitted post-M3); contracts validate against features; etc.
- Migration: existing artifacts (obol's pre-T85 features) may have invalid references. Validation needs a 'strict mode' flag or migration grace period.

Catches the slug mismatch at emission time, not iteration time. Better feedback loop than the current 'orphan tickets get silently dropped from per_item iteration' behavior.

Subsumes the in-the-immediate-fix (T1 in the option-1/2/3 conversation): option 1 (ticket-side source-of-truth lookup) shipped; this is option 2.

Validation: a tdd-design run that tries to emit a feature with tickets:['nonexistent-slug'] should reject the write, surface a useful error, and let the team retry.

items.title: Cross-registry auto-linking: registry-level update of feature.tickets after M3
items.description:
Per the obol slug-mismatch thread: even with registry validation (the P2 follow-up), feature.tickets is awkward because it gets emitted at M2 time before M3 has produced any tickets. The cleanest semantic would be: after M3 (decomposition) completes, the registry auto-updates each feature's tickets list to point at the actual emitted ticket slugs. Bidirectional reference becomes automatic and always-correct.

Requires features to be MUTABLE post-emission, which we've been keeping immutable (frozen Pydantic models, append-only registry semantics). Trade-offs:

Option A: full mutability — registry.write() supports overwrite for specific fields. Simpler but breaks the audit trail (who changed feature.tickets and when?).

Option B: emit a 'feature-amendment' artifact each time feature.tickets gets updated, append to a separate registry. Audit trail preserved; downstream readers compute current feature.tickets by walking the amendment chain. More complex.

Option C: stop storing feature.tickets entirely; compute it on-the-fly by reverse-indexing ticket.sources. Aligns with option 1 (which shipped) but more invasive — every reader of feature.tickets needs updating.

Recommendation: when this item gets prioritized, audit current feature.tickets readers first. If most are downstream lookups (M5 contracts, M6 tea party, M8 review), option C is cleanest — compute, don't store. If some are operator-facing (dashboard renders feature.tickets in detail), option B preserves the audit story.

Lower priority than the P2 validation item; option 1's ticket-side lookup is sufficient for the substrate to work correctly, this just makes feature.tickets cosmetic match reality.

items.title: Project context memory: authoritative project-level facts
items.description:
A .wonderland/project.yaml (or similar) carrying authoritative facts about THIS project that all meetings see in their seed context. Distinct from per-run directives (operator's intent for this run) and from the existing codex item b50df6af-8be2-4076-8bd8-c40d3746a64f (Caterpillar's living build-state document) — this is project-level ground truth, write-once-by-operator-or-skeleton-detection, read-only to agents.

Motivating problem: Cat's M4 ADR drift in r41-r42 obol. Operator said "Build a TUI dashboard" — Cat shipped FastAPI/React. Analysis 040 confirmed this isn't just an information-availability bug (ed082bd surfaces directive verbatim into M4 seed context); it's a structural gap. The stack should be a project-level invariant the team CANNOT unilaterally violate, not a directive sentence anyone has to remember to re-read.

Proposed shape:
  stack:
    runtime: tui | web | cli | mobile | service
    language: python | typescript | rust | go
    ui_framework: textual | react | clap | ...
    storage: sqlite | postgres | filesystem | ...
    test_framework: pytest | vitest | cargo test | ...
  entry_point: src/.../main.py
  conventions: |
    Free-form prose constraints agents read. Diff-based writes
    preferred. Tests in tests/. Etc.

Loaded as a seed kind (similar to directive — uses the seeds_fallback machinery shipped in ed082bd) so any meeting can request 'from: any kinds: [project_context]'. M4 (architecture) and M8 (review) are the obvious consumers.

Authority — the YAML alone isn't load-bearing without constitutional weight. For 'TUI' to actually constrain Cat, his §V/§VI needs a clause: 'project_context.stack is architectural ground truth; ADRs that contradict it are invalid by construction.' Without that, this is an information-availability fix that works most of the time but not when Cat has a strong prior.

Population path:
- Greenfield: skeleton picker writes project.yaml from the chosen template (P8.6 territory, already on the roadmap).
- Existing codebase: stack-detection routine introspects pyproject.toml/package.json/Cargo.toml/etc. and proposes a YAML the operator confirms. Same code, different entry point.
- Operator can edit by hand at any time.

Design questions:
  (a) One file with both project-context AND codex sections (merging with b50df6af), or two files? Different lifecycles suggest two; ergonomics suggest one. Decide when implementing.
  (b) What's the minimal field set? Start with stack-only and grow. Resist scope creep into 'team philosophy' / 'project goals' — those belong in directives.
  (c) Does M8's review check project_context as part of cross-ticket coherence (analysis 040 frame)? Probably yes — adds a 'does the implementation honor the stack' check to the existing 'does the implementation match the contract' check.
  (d) How does this interact with adopting an existing non-Wonderland repo? P8.6 covers skeleton-picker; the stack-detection routine populates project.yaml as part of adopt.

Cross-references:
- b50df6af: shared project memory (codex) — overlapping concern, different lifecycle
- f0e4afea (done): scaffolding-as-feature (project skeletons) — populates project.yaml on greenfield
- P8.6 'New-project spinup' (README status): stack-detection routine — populates project.yaml on adopt
- Analysis 040: cross-ticket coherence; M8 review scope expansion benefits from project_context

Why P1: this is the structural fix for the M4-drift class of failures (also closes the door on Cat ignoring 'TUI'); it's also a hard prerequisite for using Wonderland in existing codebases (P8.6's stack-detection has nowhere to write its output without it).

items.title: Rabbit feature merge/delete capability for M2 dedupe
items.description:
M2 (composition) can ship duplicate features when Rabbit revises mid-meeting — observed in the May 10 obol run after the post-T88 reshape: 4 first-pass features + 4 refined-pass features ended up on disk, both batches having the same ``sources`` field. The substrate has no merge or delete affordance, so the operator has to manually queue the right batch (or rm features by hand).

Two shapes worth considering:

1. New Rabbit decision type — ``revise_features`` payload like {"keep": [slug], "drop": [slug, slug, ...]} that the substrate translates into file deletes + metadata updates. Lets Rabbit consciously dedupe at commit time.

2. Auto-dedupe at M2 close — substrate detects features with overlapping sources and keeps the latest one. Operator-invisible. Risk: surprising; Rabbit's intent to ship two distinct features (with same source) gets silently overridden.

Probably (1) — explicit operator control via Rabbit's decision schema preserves intent. (2) is a safety net.

Pairs with the operator-question affordance from 2cdb3c8: when Rabbit has shipped duplicate features, ``question_to_operator`` could ask "I have two variants of the dashboard feature — keep both, merge, or pick one?" before committing to revise. That's lighter weight than a new schema and uses existing machinery.

Filed as P2 — not urgent (operator can manually dedupe), but worth doing before the next greenfield project.
